Stage 3 · Reading

The photograph that split the internet

One badly lit picture, thirteen thousand people, and what your eyes are actually doing.

👀👗
1 · Before you read. When two people describe the same thing differently, what do you usually assume?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

The photograph that split the internet

Written for this course, from Lafer-Sousa, Hermann & Conway, Current Biology 25(13), 2015, and Wallisch, ‘Illumination assumptions account for individual differences…’, Journal of Vision 17(4), 2017.

1It is not a good photograph. A small, badly lit, slightly blurred image of a dress on a hanger, taken at a wedding in Scotland and posted online in February 2015, it is overexposed at the top, where the window is, and murky at the bottom. The fabric is smooth and heavy; the lace running down it has a sharp repeating pattern; and the light source, which is the whole problem, is not visible in the frame at all.

2Within a day, several million people were arguing about it. Some observed a long, pale white dress with dull gold lace. Others saw a dark blue dress with hard black lace and could not understand what anybody else was talking about. Households divided. People sent the picture to each other expecting agreement and got a fight. The illusion was not that one group was careless; both groups were looking hard.

3Two facts settled quickly. The real garment is blue and black — that can be checked, and it was. And a group of American researchers, publishing within months, used the word “striking” in their title for the individual differences the photograph revealed, which is unusual language for a scientific paper and tells you how odd the result seemed. Normal vision was producing two incompatible answers from one small rectangle of colour.

4The explanation arrived in 2017, from a survey of more than thirteen thousand people. The question that mattered was not about colour at all: it was what viewers assumed about the light. Four out of five of those who thought the dress had been photographed in shadow saw it as white and gold, because a brain that assumes cool blue daylight subtracts blue and leaves warm colours behind. Anybody who assumed ordinary yellow indoor lighting subtracted yellow instead, and was left with blue and black — which is what the dress is.

5Then came the strange part. The researcher asked participants when they got up, and found that early risers, who spend their waking hours under a bright blue sky, were significantly more likely to see white and gold, while night owls, whose long evenings are spent under warm artificial light, tended to see blue and black. A lifetime of ordinary illumination had quietly set the assumption. Age and sex mattered far less.

6What this reveals is that vision is not a recording. Your eyes receive light that has reflected off an object, and the object’s colour and the colour of the lamp arrive mixed together; the brain has to remove one to report the other, and it does this constantly and without asking. It is the same machinery that tells you a half-submerged wooden oar is straight rather than bent, that a solid white shirt is still white at sunset, and that one twinkling orange light on dark water is a single lamp rather than twenty. Almost always it is right. On one overexposed photograph it was not, and for once you could spot the working.

Text A · A bad photograph, described

Written for this course, from Lafer-Sousa, Hermann & Conway, Current Biology 25(13), 2015.

It is not a good photograph. A small, badly lit, slightly blurred image of a dress on a hanger, taken at a wedding in Scotland and posted online in February 2015, it is overexposed at the top, where the window is, and murky at the bottom. The fabric is smooth and heavy; the lace running down it has a sharp repeating pattern; and the light source, which is the whole problem, is not visible in the frame at all.

Within a day, several million people were arguing about it. Some observed a long, pale white dress with dull gold lace. Others saw a dark blue dress with hard black lace and could not understand what anybody else was talking about. Households divided. People sent the picture to each other expecting agreement and got a fight. The illusion was not that one group was careless; both groups were looking hard, and each could describe in detail what the other was failing to see.

Two facts settled quickly. The real garment is blue and black — that can be checked, and it was. And a group of American researchers, publishing within months, used the word “striking” in their title for the individual differences the photograph revealed, which is unusual language for a scientific paper and tells you how odd the result seemed to people who study vision for a living. Normal, healthy vision was producing two incompatible answers from one small rectangle of colour, and no eye test in existence would have told you which answer a given person was about to give, because nothing was wrong with anybody’s eyes.

Text B · What your brain subtracts

Written for this course, from Wallisch, Journal of Vision 17(4), 2017.

The explanation arrived in 2017, from a survey of more than thirteen thousand people. The question that mattered was not about colour at all: it was what viewers assumed about the light. Four out of five of those who thought the dress had been photographed in shadow saw it as white and gold, because a brain that assumes cool blue daylight subtracts blue and leaves warm colours behind. Anybody who assumed ordinary yellow indoor lighting subtracted yellow instead, and was left with blue and black — which is what the dress is.

Then came the strange part. The researcher asked participants when they got up, and found that early risers, who spend their waking hours under a bright blue sky, were significantly more likely to see white and gold, while night owls, whose long evenings are spent under warm artificial light, tended to see blue and black. A lifetime of ordinary illumination had quietly set the assumption. Age and sex mattered far less.

What this reveals is that vision is not a recording. Your eyes receive light that has reflected off an object, and the object’s colour and the colour of the lamp arrive mixed together; the brain has to remove one to report the other, and it does this constantly and without asking. It is the same machinery that tells you a half-submerged wooden oar is straight rather than bent, that a solid white shirt is still white at sunset, and that one twinkling orange light on dark water is a single lamp rather than twenty. Almost always it is right. On one overexposed photograph it was not, and for once you could spot the working.

Stage 4 · Order of adjectives

Eight slots, always in the same order

Nobody chooses this order; everybody follows it. Two adjectives out of sequence make a sentence sound broken even when every word is right.

Three practical rules. One: three adjectives before a noun is the comfortable maximum; beyond that, move some after the noun (a bench, old and half-submerged in shadow). Two: no commas between adjectives from different slots (a small red plastic chair), but commas between two opinion words (a strange, beautiful room). Three: and appears only between adjectives after the verb (the bench is old and wooden), not before the noun.

1 · Read the explanation.
The order of adjectives

The sequence. Opinion → size → physical quality → shape → age → colour → origin → material → purpose → noun. A beautiful small smooth round old grey Italian marble coffee table uses every slot at once, which no English speaker would ever write, but the order is exactly that.

Why it matters. The order is not logical and cannot be reasoned out; it is stored as habit. Because of that, a reader hears a wrong order immediately, in the way you hear a wrong note. A plastic red small chair means the same thing and sounds broken.

Opinion versus fact. Opinion words (beautiful, horrible, striking, comfortable) always come before all the fact words. If you have two opinion words, separate them with a comma: a strange, beautiful room.

Commas and and. Between adjectives from different slots, no comma: a small red plastic chair. After a verb, use and before the last one: the chair was small, red and plastic. Do not write a small and red chair.

How many. Two is normal, three is the practical limit. For more, move the extra information behind the noun: a wooden bench, old and half-submerged in shadow, or use a relative clause.

Participles behave like material words. Painted, polished, curved and half-submerged sit near the noun: a large painted grey rectangle, a smooth curved surface.

The commonest errors at this level
  • a red small chair — size before colour, always.
  • a wooden old bench — age before material.
  • a small and red chair — no and before the noun.
  • a beautiful, small, red, plastic chair — commas only between opinion words.
  • Four or five adjectives in a row, which is grammatical and unreadable.

Two things to watch

1 — Opinion first, material last. If you remember only the two ends of the sequence, most strings of two or three come out right.

2 — When in doubt, use two. A beautiful old bench is better English than a correct five-adjective chain.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Ordering four adjectives step by step

The words: chair — and you want to say it is plastic, red, small and ugly.

Step 1 — find the opinion. Ugly is what you think, not what the chair is. It goes first.

Step 2 — put the facts in slot order. Size (small) → colour (red) → material (plastic).

Step 3 — count. Four adjectives is one too many for comfort. Either drop the opinion, or move it: a small red plastic chair, and an ugly one.

Step 4 — check the commas. No commas between different slots. The result: an ugly small red plastic chair is correct but heavy; a small red plastic chair is what you would actually write.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Eight slots, and nobody chooses the order

1 opinion (beautiful, striking, horrible) → 2 size (large, small, long) → 3 physical quality (smooth, rough, sharp) → 4 shape (curved, square, flat) → 5 age (old, new, ten-year-old) → 6 colour (grey, dark blue) → 7 origin (Italian, Kazakh, northern) → 8 material (wooden, glass, painted) → then purpose → then the noun.

a beautiful old wooden bench (1, 5, 8) · a small red plastic chair (2, 6, 8) · an old Kazakh silver ring (5, 7, 8) · a small old running shoe (2, 5, purpose). Nobody learns this consciously as a native speaker, and everybody follows it: two adjectives out of sequence make a phrase sound foreign even when every word is right.

How to avoid needing the list

Three or four adjectives before a noun is the practical ceiling, and good writers rarely use more than three. Where you have more to say, English has two escapes.

Move the extras after the noun: a wooden bench, old and half-submerged in shadow. This is a standard descriptive move, and it gives the extra adjectives their own stress. Put some after the verb: the bench is old and wooden — and note that and appears here but not between adjectives before a noun: a beautiful and old and wooden bench.

Two opinion adjectives may sit together with a comma between them: a strange, beautiful room. That comma is the signal that both are opinions rather than a sequence through the slots.

Errors to watch: a wooden old beautiful bench → a beautiful old wooden bench · a red small chair → a small red chair · a Kazakh old silver ring → an old Kazakh silver ring · a beautiful and old bench before a noun → drop the and.

1 · Read the model description.
Model · a place described twice

From the entrance, the market hall is a single enormous grey space with a glass roof and about forty identical stalls. The light comes down in flat columns, the floor reflects them, and the whole building reads as clean, modern and slightly cold. Most visitors take one photograph from the steps and leave with that impression.

Ten minutes inside, almost none of it is true. The roof is not glass but painted panels with two real skylights; what looks like a smooth concrete floor is old worn stone under a thin layer of dust, and the stalls are not identical at all. Six of them are pre-war: heavy wooden frames, hand-painted signs, deep shelves cut for objects nobody sells any more. The rest were built in the nineties from cheap metal tubing and copy the old ones badly.

The most striking thing is at the back, and it is not visible from the steps. Behind the last row there is a small blue tiled fountain, dry for thirty years, with a wide stone rim worn into a curve by people sitting on it. Nobody photographs it. Ask ten regular shoppers what is at the back of the hall and half of them will describe a wall.

The building is not cold, then, and it is not modern. It is an old market with a new coat on it, and the difference is entirely visible if you stand still for two minutes instead of one.
